blocks.text: 1. Introduction

If you have ever written a SQL query with a JOIN clause, you already understand ninety percent of what pd.merge does. Pandas gives you the exact same tool for combining two DataFrames, except instead of writing SQL against a database, you are calling a function against two tables sitting in memory.

This lesson picks up right where Pandas Fundamentals left off. You already know how to load data, inspect it, filter it, and clean it up. Real projects rarely hand you one tidy table though. Customer records live in one file, order history lives in another, and product prices live somewhere else entirely. Getting real work done means stitching these pieces back together, and pd.merge is the primary tool for doing exactly that.

By the end of this lesson you will know how to line up two DataFrames on a shared key, control exactly what happens to rows that do not have a match on the other side, and clean up the small messes that show up when column names collide. The centerpiece is a worked example merging a customers table with an orders table, which is about as close to real work as an example gets.
2. The Join Mental Model

A join is a simple idea wearing a slightly intimidating name. You have two tables. Each one has a column that holds the same kind of value, a customer id, a product code, an employee number, whatever it is. A join lines up rows from the two tables wherever that value matches, and glues the matching rows together into one wider row.

This is precisely what SQL's JOIN clause does, and pd.merge was deliberately designed to feel familiar to anyone who already knows SQL. The mapping between the two is close enough that you can basically translate one into the other in your head.

items: SELECT * FROM customers JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id maps to pd.merge(customers, orders, left_on='id', right_on='customer_id')
INNER JOIN maps to how='inner', which is also the default in pandas
FULL OUTER JOIN maps to how='outer'

code.content:
import pandas as pd

pd.merge(customers, orders, on='customer_id')

blocks.text: That one line does the same job as writing out a full JOIN in SQL, minus the semicolon. The rest of this lesson is about the knobs pandas gives you to control exactly how that line behaves.

blocks.caption: pd.merge mirrors the SQL JOIN you probably already know.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270137-328212083.png

blocks.title: Merging is about values, not position
blocks.content: pd.merge lines rows up by comparing the values in the key column, never by row position or index label. Two DataFrames can be sorted completely differently, have completely different lengths, and still merge correctly, because pandas is matching on content, not location. That is different from some of the row stacking tools you will see later in this module, so it is worth keeping straight early.

blocks.text: 3. The on Parameter

The on parameter tells pd.merge which column to use as the shared key. You pass it the column name as a string, and pandas uses the values in that column, on both sides, to figure out which rows belong together. It only works cleanly when both DataFrames use the exact same column name for the key, which happens more often than you might expect in real datasets that came from the same source system.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

customers = pd.DataFrame({
    'customer_id': [1, 2, 3, 4],
    'name': ['Aditi', 'Rohan', 'Meera', 'Kabir']
})

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    'order_id': [101, 102, 103],
    'customer_id': [1, 1, 3],
    'amount': [250, 400, 90]
})

merged = pd.merge(customers, orders, on='customer_id')
print(merged)

#    customer_id   name  order_id  amount
# 0            1  Aditi       101     250
# 1            1  Aditi       102     400
# 2            3  Meera       103      90

blocks.text: Notice that Aditi shows up twice. She placed two orders, so her customer row gets duplicated once for each matching order row. That is normal and expected. A merge does not deduplicate anything on its own, it just lines up every combination of matching rows between the two sides.

blocks.caption: Two DataFrames, one shared key column, one merged result.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270137-560347555.png

If you skip the on parameter entirely, pandas tries to be helpful and merges on every column name the two DataFrames have in common. That can work fine for a quick script, but it is fragile. Two DataFrames from different teams or different points in a pipeline can easily pick up an extra shared column name by accident, silently changing what your merge actually does.

blocks.title: Always name your key explicitly
blocks.content: Passing on='customer_id' costs you nothing and makes the merge self documenting. Relying on pandas to auto detect shared columns is one of those things that works fine until the day it quietly does not, usually right when someone adds a new column to one of the source tables. Treat on as mandatory in any code you plan to keep around.

blocks.text: 4. left_on and right_on for Differently Named Keys

Real datasets rarely agree on naming conventions. One system calls it emp_id, another calls the same thing employee_id, and neither team is going to rename their column just to make your merge tidier. This is exactly what left_on and right_on are for. Instead of one shared on name, you tell pandas which column to use from the left DataFrame and which column to use from the right DataFrame separately.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

employees = pd.DataFrame({
    'emp_id': [1, 2, 3],
    'name': ['Zoya', 'Farhan', 'Ishita']
})

departments = pd.DataFrame({
    'employee_id': [1, 2, 3],
    'dept': ['Engineering', 'Sales', 'Design']
})

merged = pd.merge(employees, departments, left_on='emp_id', right_on='employee_id')
print(merged)

#    emp_id    name  employee_id         dept
# 0       1    Zoya            1  Engineering
# 1       2  Farhan            2        Sales
# 2       3  Ishita            3       Design

blocks.text: The result keeps both key columns, emp_id and employee_id, sitting right next to each other with identical values. Pandas has no way of knowing you consider them the same field, so it keeps both. Most people drop the redundant one right after the merge with a call to drop, just to keep the table clean.

blocks.alt: left_on and right_on for Differently Named Keys
blocks.caption: left_on and right_on line up key columns that are named differently on each side.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270457-696463872.png
5. The Four Join Types

The how parameter is where pd.merge really earns the SQL comparison. It controls what happens to rows that do not find a match on the other side, and pandas gives you exactly four choices: inner, outer, left, and right. Picking the right one is often the difference between a report that quietly drops real customers and one that accounts for every single one of them.
5.1 Inner Join

inner is the default, so it is what you get if you leave how out entirely. An inner join keeps a row in the result only if its key value exists on both sides. If a customer has no orders, that customer disappears from the result completely, because there is nothing on the orders side to line up against. Inner joins are great for reports where you only care about records that have activity on both sides.

blocks.caption: An inner join keeps only the rows whose key exists on both sides.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270458-577680908.png
5.2 Outer Join

outer keeps everything. Every row from the left DataFrame and every row from the right DataFrame ends up in the result, whether it found a match or not. Wherever a row has no counterpart on the other side, pandas fills in NaN for all the columns that would have come from that missing side. Outer joins are the right choice when you need a complete picture and cannot afford to silently lose records from either table.

blocks.caption: An outer join keeps every row from both sides and fills the gaps with NaN.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270459-557657324.png
5.3 Left Join

left keeps every row from the left DataFrame, no exceptions, and only pulls in matching data from the right DataFrame where it exists. Unmatched right side columns become NaN. This is the join you reach for when one table is your source of truth, customers for instance, and you want to see every single one of them regardless of whether they have any related activity.

blocks.caption: A left join keeps every left row and fills unmatched right side data with NaN.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270459-234278816.png
5.4 Right Join

right is the mirror image of left. Every row from the right DataFrame survives, and unmatched left side columns become NaN. In practice, most people reach for left far more often than right, simply because it is usually easier to reorder your arguments and use left than to remember which side right refers to. Functionally the two are identical, just flipped.

blocks.caption: A right join is the mirror image of a left join.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270459-219467586.png

blocks.text: 6. Worked Example: The Same Two DataFrames, Four Ways

Reading about four join types is one thing. Watching the exact same two DataFrames produce four different results is what actually makes the differences click. Here are two small DataFrames that only partially overlap on their key column.

id 1 only exists on the left, id 4 only exists on the right, and id 2 and id 3 exist on both sides. That overlap pattern is exactly what makes the four join types diverge from each other. Watch what happens to id 1 and id 4 in each version.

code.content:
pd.merge(left_df, right_df, on='id', how='inner')

#    id   name  score
# 0   2   Beta     88
# 1   3  Gamma     92

blocks.text: Inner keeps only id 2 and id 3. id 1 and id 4 are both gone, because neither one has a match on the other side.

code.content:
pd.merge(left_df, right_df, on='id', how='outer')

#    id   name  score
# 0   1  Alpha    NaN
# 1   2   Beta   88.0
# 2   3  Gamma   92.0
# 3   4    NaN   75.0

blocks.text: Outer keeps all four ids. id 1 gets a NaN for score because it has no match on the right, and id 4 gets a NaN for name because it has no match on the left. Notice that score becomes a float column here. Pandas upgrades an integer column to float the moment it needs to hold a NaN, since NaN itself is a floating point value.

code.content:
pd.merge(left_df, right_df, on='id', how='left')

#    id   name  score
# 0   1  Alpha    NaN
# 1   2   Beta   88.0
# 2   3  Gamma   92.0

blocks.text: Left keeps id 1, 2 and 3, all three rows that live on the left side. id 4 is dropped entirely since it only exists on the right, and the left DataFrame never had a row for it in the first place.

code.content:
pd.merge(left_df, right_df, on='id', how='right')

#    id   name  score
# 0   2   Beta     88
# 1   3  Gamma     92
# 2   4    NaN     75

blocks.text: Right keeps id 2, 3 and 4, all three rows that live on the right side, and drops id 1 for the same reason left dropped id 4.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Join Type","Rows In Result","id Values Present","NaN Introduced"],"rows":[["Inner","2","2 and 3","No"],["Outer","4","1, 2, 3 and 4","Yes, for id 1 with no score and id 4 with no name"],["Left","3","1, 2 and 3","Yes, for id 1 with no score"],["Right","3","2, 3 and 4","Yes, for id 4 with no name"]]}

blocks.title: Same inputs, four different row counts
blocks.content: This example is worth bookmarking. Every time you are unsure which join type to reach for, come back to this exact pattern, two DataFrames with a partial overlap, and mentally run through what each of the four options keeps and what each one throws away.

blocks.text: 7. Handling Column Name Collisions with suffixes

Key columns are not the only columns that can share a name. Plenty of real merges involve two DataFrames that both happen to have, say, a price column or a date column that means something different on each side. When that happens, pandas cannot just keep one price column, since that would silently throw away real data, so it renames both.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

store_a = pd.DataFrame({
    'product_id': [1, 2],
    'price': [10, 20]
})

store_b = pd.DataFrame({
    'product_id': [1, 2],
    'price': [12, 18]
})

merged = pd.merge(store_a, store_b, on='product_id')
print(merged)

#    product_id  price_x  price_y
# 0           1       10       12
# 1           2       20       18

blocks.text: By default pandas tags the colliding columns with _x for the left DataFrame and _y for the right DataFrame. That works, but price_x and price_y do not tell anyone reading your code which price came from which store. Naming them explicitly with the suffixes parameter fixes that.

blocks.alt: Handling Column Name Collisions with suffixes
blocks.caption: A shared non key column name gets resolved with suffixes.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270460-257435710.png

code.content:
merged = pd.merge(store_a, store_b, on='product_id', suffixes=('_store_a', '_store_b'))
print(merged)

#    product_id  price_store_a  price_store_b
# 0           1             10             12
# 1           2             20             18

blocks.title: Do not settle for _x and _y
blocks.content: The default suffixes are a reasonable fallback, but in any merge that is going to live in real code, pass suffixes explicitly. Future you, or whoever reads this next, will not have to go dig through both source DataFrames just to figure out what price_x actually means.

blocks.text: 8. The indicator Parameter

Sometimes a merge does not produce the row count you expected, and you need to figure out why. Setting indicator=True adds an extra column called _merge to the result, and that column tells you exactly which side each row came from, left_only, right_only, or both.

code.content:
merged = pd.merge(left_df, right_df, on='id', how='outer', indicator=True)
print(merged)

#    id   name  score      _merge
# 0   1  Alpha    NaN   left_only
# 1   2   Beta   88.0        both
# 2   3  Gamma   92.0        both
# 3   4    NaN   75.0  right_only

blocks.caption: The indicator column labels exactly which side each row came from.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270460-202468072.png

This is one of the fastest ways to debug a merge that looks off. Instead of squinting at NaN values scattered across the result trying to reconstruct what happened, you can filter directly on the _merge column and immediately see, for example, every row that only exists in the right DataFrame.

blocks.title: A debugging tool, not a permanent fixture
blocks.content: indicator is genuinely useful while you are figuring out why a merge produced more or fewer rows than you expected. Most people drop the _merge column once they are satisfied the merge is doing what it should, since it is not usually meaningful to whoever consumes the final table.

blocks.text: 9. Catching Surprises with validate

The validate parameter checks an assumption about the relationship between your two DataFrames before it lets the merge through. You tell it what kind of relationship you expect, one_to_one, one_to_many, many_to_one, or many_to_many, and pandas raises an error immediately if your data does not actually match that shape.

customer_id 1 shows up twice in orders, because Aditi placed two separate orders. That is completely normal data, but it violates a one to one assumption, so pandas stops you right there instead of quietly producing a result you did not expect. Swapping in validate='one_to_many' would let this exact merge through without complaint, since one customer legitimately maps to many orders.

blocks.caption: validate catches a one to many surprise before it becomes a silent bug.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270461-563021169.png

blocks.title: Cheap insurance against silent bugs
blocks.content: validate costs you one keyword argument and catches a whole category of bugs where a merge quietly multiplies rows because a key you assumed was unique actually was not. Any time you expect a clean one to one relationship between two tables, add validate='one_to_one' and let pandas confirm it for you instead of finding out three steps later when your row counts look wrong.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example: Customers and Orders

Time to put all of this together on a scenario that looks like real work. You have a customers table and an orders table, and two different people on your team need two different answers out of the same two tables.
10.1 Setting Up the Data

Four customers, three orders. Aditi placed two orders, Meera placed one, and Rohan and Kabir have not ordered anything yet. Keep that last detail in mind, it is exactly what makes this example useful.
10.2 Inner Join for a Report
Finance wants a report of every order along with the customer who placed it. They only care about orders that actually happened, so an inner join is exactly the right tool.

code.content:
report = pd.merge(customers, orders, on='customer_id', how='inner')
print(report)

blocks.text: The result lines up perfectly with what finance asked for.

blocks.caption: An inner join on customer_id keeps only customers who actually ordered something.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270461-928524411.png
Rohan and Kabir never show up here, and that is correct behavior, not a bug. They have no orders, so there is nothing for an inner join to match them against.
10.3 Left Join to Find Customers With Zero Orders

Marketing has the opposite question. They want to find customers who have never placed an order, so they can target them with a promotion. An inner join is useless here, since it drops exactly the rows marketing cares about. A left join is what they need instead.

code.content:
all_customers = pd.merge(customers, orders, on='customer_id', how='left')
zero_order_customers = all_customers[all_customers['order_id'].isna()]
print(zero_order_customers)

blocks.text: Merging with how='left' keeps every customer, then filtering for the rows where order_id is missing isolates exactly the customers who never matched anything on the orders side.

blocks.alt: Left Join to Find Customers With Zero Orders
blocks.caption: A left join keeps every customer, so unmatched rows reveal who never ordered.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270461-804118000.png

Rohan and Kabir show up cleanly, with NaN standing in for the order_id and amount they never generated. Same two source tables as the inner join above, same on column, one changed parameter, and two teams get two completely different, completely correct answers.
11. Recap

items: pd.merge combines two DataFrames by matching values in a shared key column, the same core idea as a SQL JOIN.
Use on when both DataFrames name the key column the same way, and left_on plus right_on when they do not.
how controls what happens to unmatched rows: inner drops them, outer keeps everything and fills gaps with NaN, left keeps every left row, right keeps every right row.
suffixes rename colliding non key column names so the result stays readable.
indicator adds a _merge column that tells you exactly which side each row came from, invaluable for debugging.
validate checks the relationship you expect between the two DataFrames and raises an error early if reality does not match.

blocks.text: The merge, join, and concat trio covers almost every way you will ever need to combine data in pandas. This lesson covered merge in depth. The next two build on the exact same mental model, so the join mental model you just built is going to keep paying off.
